items.title: Susumu Tonegawa (1939–2026)
items.author: Peter Mombaerts
items.content: <article>On a cold January weekend morning in a picturesque Swiss town, a 36-year-old Japanese scientist went to his lab to check the results of an experiment he had designed to answer a century-old immunology question: how do animals generate antibodies to countless antigens? He had run a large gel electrophoresis to separate DNA fragments from the genome of a mouse B cell tumor called a myeloma in parallel with DNA fragments from the genome of embryos of the same mouse strain. He had generated these DNA fragments using the brand-new technology of restriction enzyme digestion, then labeled the relevant fragments with radioactive myeloma RNA, which is enriched for immunoglobulin light-chain RNA.</article>

items.title: Educational neuroscience in times of artificial intelligence
items.author: Suzanne Dikker
items.content: <article>In this issue of Neuron, Peng et al. show that introductory conversations, with either a human instructor or her AI avatar, align students’ brain patterns and improve comprehension of difficult lecture content. The study both answers and raises important questions about AI in education.</article>

items.title: Specialized vascular niches preserve adult neural circuits
items.author: Dario Bonanomi
items.content: <article>In this issue of Neuron, Zhu et al. show that Netrin-4 from specialized arterial smooth muscle cells restrains a latent death pathway in a subset of adult sympathetic neurons, revealing a neurovascular mechanism that selectively maintains mature neural circuits through spatially restricted survival signals.</article>
